title: Kierkegaard
hookLine: a Danish philosopher: faith is a leap, and life is lived forward but understood backward

cards: Hindsight is a strange gift. Looking back, a breakup can make sense, or a job that fell through, or a dreaded move that turned out to be where everything started. At the time, there is only the edge, and not knowing.
A Danish writer in Copenhagen put that into one of his journals, and readers still quote it: life can only be understood backward, but it has to be lived forward.
He was a philosopher, a sharp critic of comfortable churchgoing, and a Christian who thought real faith asks for everything. Today: Kierkegaard.

teach.b: Søren Kierkegaard wrote much of his work under made-up names, each a different voice arguing a different view, so readers would have to think for themselves.
The journal line is his own, paraphrased here: philosophers are right that life must be understood backward, but they forget the other half.
It must be lived forward, and you never get to stand still long enough to understand it all before the next step. That's where faith comes in.
In Fear and Trembling, written under the name Johannes de silentio, John of silence, he circles one story: Abraham, called to take his son Isaac up Mount Moriah.
The book's author says he can admire Abraham, but cannot understand him. Faith, here, goes where the argument can't follow.

Hebrews sums up Abraham's faith from its first step, in the King James Bible: "By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went."
For Kierkegaard, that is faith: not a conclusion at the end of an argument, but a step taken before you can see where it leads.

teach.h: FAITH AS A LEAP, NOT A CONCLUSION.
teach.b: He wrote about it as a leap, and some readers sum up his whole idea as the leap of faith.
He had little patience for a Christianity that cost nothing; in comfortable Denmark, he thought, it was too easy to be a Christian by birth certificate.

Real faith, he argued, is a personal, lived risk, made by one person standing before God. His challenge to readers: admire Abraham from a safe distance, or step out yourself, not knowing whither you go.

how: Christian thinkers, preachers and students read Kierkegaard on faith as a personal risk, especially Fear and Trembling and its reading of Abraham.

games.q: you're Abraham. God calls you to leave home for a place you'll receive later. you don't know where it is. what do you do?
o: wait until the destination is clear.
send someone ahead to check first.
games.why: Hebrews says Abraham obeyed and "went out, not knowing whither he went." for Kierkegaard, that's what faith looks like.

practice: Bring to mind a decision you've been circling, waiting to understand it fully first: a conversation, an application, an apology. You won't see the whole path from here, so name only the next forward step, in a few words.
If you pray, ask for courage to step without seeing; if you don't, simply hold the step.

wordCard.voice: Kierkegaard. A Danish philosopher who wrote that life is understood backward but lived forward, and who saw faith as a leap, like Abraham's.

carryVoice: Your line: lived forward. The understanding can come later, after the step. See you tomorrow.
